item.title: The 8 Systems Every Contracting Business Needs (and Which to Build First)
item.dc:creator: Bolt Answering Content Team
item.description: A contracting business needs eight systems, not hundreds of procedures. Here are the eight, and the two to build first.
item.content:encoded:
Every successful contracting business has eight systems: marketing, sales, estimating, project management, field management, office management, bookkeeping and people. You don’t need all eight at once. Start with referrals and reviews, then change orders and job costing, and add one more system each quarter.

If you’ve tried to “get organized” and quit three weeks in, you probably tried to fix everything at once. A contracting business doesn’t need hundreds of procedures. It needs a few systems covering the places where work, money and people move through the company. The list was written with general contractors in mind, but a roofer, a siding crew or a handyman will recognize every piece.

What are the eight systems?

  1. Marketing. How qualified leads find you without luck: a clear picture of your ideal client, a tracked referral process, a complete Google Business Profile, a routine for asking for reviews and regular contact with past clients.
  2. Sales. How leads become signed contracts: how fast you answer, the questions you ask before anyone drives out, a site-visit checklist, how you present a proposal and a follow-up schedule. Speed matters, since a homeowner who gets voicemail often calls the next contractor. Not every lead deserves an estimate either, so check budget, timeline, decision-maker, competing bids and location before you spend a day pricing.
  3. Estimating. How you price work for profit: site-visit forms, bid requests to subs, bid comparisons, a standard estimate format, a review checklist and a record of past job costs so you aren’t guessing.
  4. Project management. How the job gets delivered: pre-construction meetings, scheduling, selections, change orders, budget tracking, homeowner updates and closeout with a punch list and warranty paperwork.
  5. Field management. How work gets done on site: daily checklists, phase-by-phase checklists, quality standards, safety procedures and daily logs.
  6. Office management. The glue: job setup, invoicing, paying vendors, collecting insurance certificates and W-9s, tracking your own license and insurance renewals, and regular meetings.
  7. Bookkeeping. A chart of accounts that fits construction, cost codes, up-to-date job costing, payroll, reconciliations and a weekly or monthly look at the numbers.
  8. People. Hiring, onboarding, reviews, accountability and what happens when someone leaves. The other seven only work if the right people run them.

How many systems are too many?

Too many systems create bloat, slow decisions and push prices up. A process nobody follows, or one that adds steps without protecting money or time, is worse than none.

Test each one with a single question: does it keep you from losing money, missing a call or redoing work? If yes, write it down. If no, skip it. You want the smallest set of checklists that lets someone else do the job the way you would.

Which system should you build first?

Spend your first month on the two with the clearest payoff.

Start with referrals and reviews. Write down how you ask for them, who tracks them and how you thank people. It costs almost nothing, and referrals are often a contractor’s cheapest leads.

Then do change orders and job costing. Contractors lose margin on scope changes that were never priced, and on jobs where nobody knew the numbers until too late. One change-order form and a weekly look at costs against budget go a long way.

After that, add one system per quarter. A year from now the business runs on paper instead of your memory.

Fast answers are the first part of a sales system to break when you’re on a roof or under a sink. Bolt Answering picks up the calls you miss, asks what the job is, where and how soon, and books it into your schedule, with your first 30 days free.

item.title: Why Your Contracting Business Stops Growing
item.dc:creator: Bolt Answering Content Team
item.description: Most contractors stall because every estimate, call and decision runs through the owner. Do the revenue-per-hour math, then hand off one task.
item.content:encoded:
Most contracting businesses stop growing because everything still runs through one person: the owner. Estimates, sales calls, schedules and problem-solving all wait on you, so revenue can’t pass what you can personally handle. The fix is to take yourself out of the middle one task at a time, starting with the one that interrupts you most.

A lot of contractors hit a number and stay there. Maybe it’s $150,000 a year, maybe $1.2 million. The work is good and the homeowners are happy, and the revenue barely moves while the owner gets more tired each season.

Why do good contractors get stuck?

Contractors who can’t do the work wash out early, so they never get far enough to get stuck. Skilled ones get stuck differently. You’re the best estimator and the best closer, and you’re the only one who knows which job is behind and which sub is about to flake. At first, being the person everybody needs feels like winning.

Then the cost shows up. You answer the phone at 5 a.m. because nobody else knows what to say. You take every sales call. Every takeoff lives in your head and the books live in a shoebox. If you’re out sick for two months, the business stops. That is a job, even if it pays well.

What is the difference between your value and the business’s value?

Some of the value in your business exists only while you’re working. Estimating, managing, solving problems and being on site all stop paying the moment you stop. The rest exists without you: written systems that run while you’re away, people who can carry them out, and a track record that shows the business works.

Only the second kind can grow past what one person can carry, and only it can be sold someday. A buyer pays for profit that keeps coming in after the owner leaves. A business that falls apart without you has little to sell.

How much revenue do you make per hour you work?

Divide your annual revenue by the hours you personally put in. Say a business brings in $1.2 million while you work 60 hours a week for 50 weeks, about 3,000 hours. That’s roughly $400 of revenue for every hour of your time.

Now suppose the same revenue runs on written systems and trained people, and you spend about 1,000 hours a year reviewing numbers and making decisions. That’s $1,200 an hour, and the business keeps running if you’re gone for a month. These numbers are an example. Use your own.

Growing past your own hours means getting more revenue out of each hour you work.

Which task should you hand off first?

Most stuck owners ask how to get more done. A better question is which part of the business could run without you.

You don’t have to answer it everywhere at once. Pick the task that interrupts you most often, such as answering new-lead calls, building estimates or chasing invoices. Write down exactly how you do it, hand it to someone (or something) with a checklist, and let it run for a month. Then pick the next one.

FAQ

Why does my contracting business stay the same size every year?

Usually because estimating, selling, scheduling and problem-solving all run through you, so revenue is capped by your hours. Growth starts when you pull one task at a time out of your head and into a checklist someone else can follow.

The task that interrupts you most often. For many pros that’s answering new-lead calls, building estimates or chasing invoices.

Yes, but only as far as your hours allow unless you write down how work gets done and hand pieces of it off. Even one handed-off task, like the phone or invoicing, frees up hours you can spend on sales and estimates.

item.title: Great at the Work but Not Getting Calls: A Fix for Solo Tradespeople
item.dc:creator: Bolt Answering Content Team
item.description: Being excellent at the work and being easy to find are two different skills, and the second one decides whether the phone rings. Skilled and quiet Plenty of…
item.content:encoded:
Being excellent at the work and being easy to find are two different skills, and the second one decides whether the phone rings.

Skilled and quiet

Plenty of solo tradespeople do careful work, have happy customers, and still go weeks between calls. The problem is rarely the trade. It is that the people who need you cannot find you, cannot reach you, or hear nothing back.

The fix is not a bigger ad budget. It is a short list of boring habits done every week.

Three places new work comes from

  1. Google. A complete Google Business Profile, a phone-friendly site and fresh reviews. This catches homeowners who need someone now.
  2. Repeat builders and managers. General contractors, property managers and apartment complexes hire the same trades again and again. Many already have a favorite, so ask to be the backup, send a short intro and your license and insurance, and check in a few times a year. Vet them too: ask how long they take to pay.
  3. Referrals. Ask every happy customer, in person, for one name. Then follow up so they remember you.

A 30-day plan

Expect results to build over months, not days.

If you are brand new on a tight budget

You do not need a big spend to start. Free or cheap first steps: a complete Google Business Profile, a one-page site with a tap-to-call button, reviews from your first customers, and a short intro to builders and property managers. Door-knocking and flyers in neighborhoods where you just finished a job still work. Avoid committing to a multi-thousand-dollar package before you have measured what brings calls.

Do not fix a quiet phone by cutting your price

Dropping your price is the tempting move, but it attracts price shoppers and squeezes your margin. Visibility, reviews and a fast answer usually do more than a discount.

Bidding is a different game

Government and large commercial jobs are found through public bid listings, where you compete against many firms on price. That is a different business from residential service work. The steps above are for the second kind.

Where Bolt fits

item.title: Communication, Books, and Growth: The Business Side of Handyman Work
item.dc:creator: Bolt Answering Content Team
item.description: Great repair skills aren’t enough to build a handyman business. Here’s how to communicate clearly, keep real books, and grow without working every evening.
item.content:encoded:
Great repair skills will not build a handyman business on their own. Three habits decide whether you end up with steady money and free evenings or a pile of stress: how you communicate, how you track your money, and how you grow.

Over-communicate, and under-promise

Misunderstandings happen all the time, and often the client heard something different from what you meant. Aim for clarity: as one handyman put it, don’t speak to be understood, speak to not be misunderstood. For anything important, say it two or three different ways and confirm that the client understands.

Then set expectations you can beat. If a job could take up to three months and you finish in three weeks, you are the hero. If you promise a flat, problem-free job, you have no room for the surprises that every real job brings. Weather, materials, and other trades all cause delays.

Be upfront about the messy parts too. Will there be dust? Do you need to hang a zip wall or run a fan? Will you spray texture and come back another day to paint? Telling clients before the work starts means they are prepared and not annoyed.

Keep real books

Every handyman has expenses, from materials bought for clients to a new radiator cap for the truck, and hopefully income to match. If you do not record both, you will not know whether the business makes money, how much tax to pay, or what you can afford to invest.

Alan Lee of The Handyman Journey admits that in his first year he did not even track how much he brought in, and he wrote invoices in Google Docs. Over time he improved, and connecting accounting software like QuickBooks Online to his bank accounts and cards now produces profit and loss statements once things are reconciled. Start with a simple system today. Better books also make it easier to set the prices covered in the previous post.

Decide how you will grow

When the work piles up, there are two main paths.

Technician-heavy growth. You hire more people to do jobs. This can bring in a bit more money, but you still handle the calls, estimates, invoices, work orders, taxes, and uniforms. You rarely clock out at five.

Admin-heavy growth. You build the office side first so you are not the bottleneck. Alan’s order of hiring was a customer service rep to answer phones, emails, and reviews, then an estimator, then a technician assistant, and then another technician. The assistant buys materials and delivers them before the technician arrives, then hauls debris away afterward. Once the admin is handled, he says, adding vans and technicians becomes a repeatable process, and he can clock out around 4:30 and skip weekends.

The trade-off is a bit less money in the short term in return for much more freedom. Whichever path you pick, write down processes for each role and take care of your team.

A note on being a business

One handyman argues that handymen are contractors and need to treat what they do as a business, or the stigma will stay. That is a useful mindset. Check your state’s rules on what a handyman may do, since they vary.

Your checklist

  • Write down how you will explain timing and mess before every job.
  • Pick accounting software and connect your bank account.
  • Track income and expenses weekly.
  • Choose a growth path before your first hire.
  • Document the one task you want off your plate first.

The first hire in an admin-first business is someone to answer the phone, and you may not be ready for that salary yet. Bolt Answering is a smart assistant that answers your calls so you can start building the admin side today. Start your free trial.

item.title: A Lead Is Only Worth What Happens When the Phone Rings
item.dc:creator: Bolt Answering Content Team
item.description: You can spend a lot to make a phone ring and still lose the job, because the job is decided in the first minutes after the call comes in. You paid for the…
item.content:encoded:
You can spend a lot to make a phone ring and still lose the job, because the job is decided in the first minutes after the call comes in.

You paid for the ring, then missed it

Every marketing channel, whether Google, referrals, ads or lead sites, ends in the same moment: a homeowner calls and someone answers or no one does.

If you are under a sink or on a roof, the answer is usually no. The caller does not leave a long voicemail. They try the next name on the list.

Speed decides who gets the job

A homeowner with a broken water heater is not shopping. They call, and whoever picks up first usually wins.

The caller is already in a hurry, and the next contractor is one tap away. Every minute you take to respond gives them a reason to move on.

Why good contractors miss calls

It is not laziness. The work itself makes you unreachable.

  • Your hands are in a wall, on a ladder or covered in something you do not want on a phone.
  • Stopping a job to answer costs time and breaks your focus.
  • Driving between jobs is not a safe time to take a call.
  • You are a solo operator, so there is no one else to pick up.

The cost is real but invisible. You never see the jobs that went to someone who answered. A simple test: look at your phone’s missed-call list for last week and count the numbers you never called back.

Is it missed calls, or a quiet phone?

A phone that has gone quiet and a phone that goes unanswered look the same from the driver’s seat. Check both. Missed calls show up in your call log. A quiet phone means fewer people are finding you at all, often because competitors with stronger websites and listings rank above you.

Fix the one you actually have: answer faster if calls come in and get missed, and work on visibility if they do not come in.

A simple fix

The fix is to make sure a person or a system picks up every call, within seconds, every time.

item.title: How to Price Handyman Jobs So You Actually Make Money
item.dc:creator: Bolt Answering Content Team
item.description: Not sure what to charge? Here’s a simple formula for working out your hourly number, plus how to handle customers who want a discount in exchange for future…
item.content:encoded:
The most common reason new handymen quit is simple: they do not charge enough. Here is a practical way to work out your rate, hold it when customers push back, and avoid the discounts that quietly drain your income.

Start with what the customer will pay, not what you would pay

It is tempting to price a job by asking what you would pay someone else to do it. That thinking does not matter. What matters is how much your customers are willing to pay to have the work done. That is supply and demand: if people will pay a certain amount for a job done well, you can charge that amount.

Work out your hourly number

Even if you never quote by the hour, everything comes down to an hourly rate, so know yours. Here is the method Alan Lee of The Handyman Journey describes:

  1. Add up all your hard costs: truck, fuel, tires, insurance, tools, software, and your own pay.
  2. Add 20 percent for a break-even cushion.
  3. Add another 20 percent for profit.
  4. Divide by the number of hours you can realistically bill in a month.

Here is an illustration with made-up numbers: $6,000 in monthly costs becomes $8,640 after both 20 percent additions. If you bill about 126 hours a month, that is roughly $69 an hour.

Do not forget efficiency

An eight-hour day is not eight billable hours. You stop for gas, run to the hardware store, answer calls, talk to the client, and take breaks. Expect about 70 to 80 percent efficiency, which means five and a half to six billable hours. Build that into your rate so you are paid for the whole day.

Quote by the job, but know your hourly rate

Keep your hourly rate in your head and not state it to clients. Handymen are split on this. One handyman charges strictly by the hour, saying a flat price tempts you to cut corners if surprises appear. Another, with more than 20 years in the trade, never worked by the hour and gave only finished labor prices, and says he made six figures every year. Pick one, but make sure your price covers the surprises. Quote materials carefully too, since prices change from day to day.

Say no to “future work” discounts

If someone says there will be lots more work if you lower your price today, be careful. Nine times out of ten that work never arrives. Quote the first job at your real price. If you go cheap, the client will expect cheap forever, and you will be known as the cheap handyman.

Let some bids go

One piece of advice: if you are not losing about half your bids because they are too high, you are not charging enough. Experienced handymen add that you should walk away from people who push you to work for nothing, since they tend to nickel and dime you afterward. Higher prices also signal value, while free work is treated as worth little.

A few ideas from working handymen

  • Charge a fee for the first visit, instead of giving free estimates, if you find that estimates eat up your time.
  • Ask for a deposit before starting jobs you are unsure about.
  • Add a surcharge for difficult jobs, such as hauling tools up a hill or working in tight spaces.
  • Look into property management companies, which one handyman says can keep you busy seven days a week.

These are individual experiences, not rules, so test them against your own market.

You can’t price a job you don’t understand, and a rushed call gives you half the details. Bolt Answering asks your customers the right questions up front, so you know the scope before you quote. Try it free.

item.title: Own Your Lead Flow: Control vs. Renting Your Customers
item.dc:creator: Bolt Answering Content Team
item.description: If a platform brings you your customers, the platform sets the terms. It can change prices, reviews and rules, and you have no say. Renting versus owning A…
item.content:encoded:
If a platform brings you your customers, the platform sets the terms. It can change prices, reviews and rules, and you have no say.

Renting versus owning

A lead marketplace is a rented storefront. The price per lead can rise, the quality can shift, and the way your reviews appear is not yours to decide. If most of your calls come from one place, you work for that place.

A business that owns its channels, a website, a Google Business Profile and a list of past customers, can dial the flow up or down and keep every relationship it builds.

What you control when you own the channel

  • Volume. More jobs than you can handle? Pause ads or raise prices. Slow month? Turn them up.
  • The first impression. Your site, photos and wording are yours.
  • Reviews. Ask every happy customer, and respond to every review.
  • The customer relationship. The phone number and name belong to you, not to a platform.

None of this is instant. A Google listing and a decent site take weeks to pay off. But the effort compounds, while lead spend resets to zero every month.

Filter out tire-kickers before you drive

A wasted site visit costs you gas and an hour. Cut those before they happen:

  • Post a rough price range for common jobs so budget shoppers opt out early.
  • Add a simple quote calculator or form that asks job type, size and timeline.
  • Ask three questions on the first call: what is the problem, when do they need it done, and have they gotten other quotes.
  • Set a minimum job size and say so.

The goal is not fewer calls. It is fewer calls that go nowhere.

Channels you own are not only online

Owned channels include your past customers, the builders and managers who hire you, and old-fashioned outreach such as knocking doors or leaving a flyer after a job. These cost time instead of per-lead fees, and the relationship stays yours. They are slower than a lead feed, but nobody reprices them.

One more caution: Google sells leads too

Google’s Local Services Ads charge per lead as well. They can work, but the same rule applies: measure cost per job won, and do not let any one paid channel become your only source of work.

Turning the dial

Owning the channel only works if you can handle what it sends. When you turn the volume up, the calls come while you are working.

item.title: How Contractors Got Found Before Google, and Why That Changed
item.dc:creator: Bolt Answering Content Team
item.description: For decades a contractor’s reputation traveled by mouth, and that still matters, but the first conversation about you now happens on a phone screen. Word of…
item.content:encoded:
For decades a contractor’s reputation traveled by mouth, and that still matters, but the first conversation about you now happens on a phone screen.

Word of mouth, then

Before the internet, a homeowner who wanted a remodel asked a neighbor, a friend or a relative who they knew. The answer was usually one of two stories: a great contractor worth calling, or a horror story to avoid.

Either way, you were found because someone vouched for you. If you did good work, the same people hired you again and told others. That is still the cheapest and best source of work.

Word of mouth, now

Homeowners still ask friends and neighbors. But the next step has changed: they check the name on their phone.

If a rival has a modern site, a complete Google listing and recent reviews, that rival gets the call even when your work is better. Few people scroll to the second page of search results. A referral that leads to an empty or outdated search result can die right there.

So referrals and search now work as one system. Referrals bring people to your name, and your online presence decides whether they call.

What a customer sees when they search for you

Search your own business name and your trade plus your town, on your phone. Then ask what a stranger would conclude.

  • Is there a Google listing with your correct phone number, hours and service area?
  • Do you have recent reviews, and do you answer them?
  • Does your site load fast on a phone, with a tap-to-call button above the fold?
  • Are there photos of real jobs rather than stock images?
  • Do the first results belong to you, or to directory and lead sites that collect contact details and resell them?

That last point matters. Directory sites often rank above individual contractors, so owning a strong listing and site is how you show up beside or above them.

A good-looking site is not the same as being found

Contractors often say they paid for a professional website and still never appear in search. Looks and visibility are separate jobs. Before paying anyone for SEO, ask what exactly they will change, how they will measure it, and what you can check yourself, such as where you rank for your trade plus your town on a phone, and how many calls come from your Google listing. Be wary of anyone who cannot explain this plainly or who guarantees first-page results.

If referrals have slowed

Many established contractors who ran on referrals for years say calls have dropped over the last decade. People talk less about who they hired and search more. You do not need to abandon word of mouth. You need a findable online presence so the referral has somewhere to land. It is also a good project to hand to a younger family member or a part-time helper.

Checklist, and the last step

  1. Claim your Google listing and fill every field.
  2. Ask each happy customer for a review, and reply to every one.
  3. Make sure your site works well on a phone.
  4. Make sure every call that comes from those places gets answered.

item.title: 5 Mistakes That Keep Handymen Underpaid (and How to Avoid Them)
item.dc:creator: Bolt Answering Content Team
item.description: Undercharging, weak communication, sloppy books: these five mistakes keep handymen underpaid. See what they are and how to fix each one.
item.content:encoded:
Six and a half years into running his own handyman business, Alan Lee of The Handyman Journey says he made plenty of mistakes, and that many other handymen are making the same ones. If you want to earn more and work fewer late nights, these are the five to watch for.

1. Not charging enough

This is the big one. If you undercharge, you cannot cover your bills, so many new handymen end up quitting and going back to a regular job. Most of us are not in this to do charity work. We are in it for financial freedom and control of our time, and neither is possible when your prices are too low. Charge what the work is worth to the customer, and do quality work so the price holds up.

2. Weak communication

Misunderstandings are common, so err on the side of over-communicating. Rephrase important points two or three different ways until the client clearly understands. Then under-promise and over-deliver. If a job could take three months and you finish in one, you are a hero. If you promised it in one and it takes three, you have a problem. Tell clients about dust, setup, and extra visits ahead of time so nothing catches them off guard.

3. Cutting your price for “future work”

Someone offers you a lot of work later if you give them a deal today. Nine times out of ten, the future work never comes, and you are the one who loses. Quote the first job at the price you need to charge. If you go low now, the client will expect low prices forever, and a reputation as the cheap guy is very hard to shake.

4. Sloppy bookkeeping

Handymen buy materials, truck parts, tools, and gas, and they bring in income. If you do not track both sides, you will not know whether you are making money or how much tax you owe. Alan admits he did not even know his first-year income. Accounting software such as QuickBooks Online, connected to your bank and cards, makes it far easier to see profit and loss.

5. Growing without a plan

Hiring a second technician sounds like the obvious way to make more, but you are still stuck with all the admin: calls, estimates, invoices, work orders, and taxes. Alan chose to grow the admin side first, so he could stop working evenings and weekends. Decide on purpose how you want to grow before you hire.

The takeaway

All five mistakes come back to treating your handyman work as a real business. Price for profit, communicate clearly, hold your prices, track your numbers, and plan your growth. The next two posts go deeper into each of these.

item.title: From Jack of All Trades to Go-To Guy: A Growth Plan for Handymen
item.dc:creator: Bolt Answering Content Team
item.description: Saying yes to every job keeps handymen stuck. Here’s a six-step plan for picking a niche, finding your ideal customer, and becoming the go-to name in your…
item.content:encoded:
Most handymen stay stuck because they say “yes” to everything. The jobs are random, the pricing is guesswork, and every week starts from zero. The fix is simple: stop being a generalist and build a business around a few services you can do fast, well, and repeat. Here’s how to turn that into a growth plan.

Step 1: Choose your niche on purpose

Look for work that commonly breaks or gets damaged in a house: holes in walls, worn doors and locks, old fixtures. Those problems never stop, and people pay to have them fixed. Choose one or two services, such as drywall plus doors, or fixtures plus fans, and commit to them for a few months.

Step 2: Aim at a specific customer

Working handymen show what this looks like in practice. One focuses on new-build homes, doing builder-grade closet shelving, 8-foot doors, and lights and fans, and plans a business card that simply says “doors, lights, shelves.” Another avoids low-paying, high-competition work such as basic TV mounting and installs slim LED recessed lights instead. A third loves storm door installs where the customer supplies the door, with an upsell on new brick molding. The pattern: a narrow offer, a clear customer, and a bit of competition avoided.

Step 3: Become the known name

The more jobs you do of one type, the more neighbors, realtors, and builders hear that you are the person for it. Ask every happy customer for a Google review and a referral, and keep your marketing message to one line. Specific beats broad: “I fix doors and locks” is easier to remember than “I do all kinds of repairs.”

Step 4: Increase profit per visit

Three levers: (1) let customers supply materials, (2) bundle related services, and (3) suggest things they didn’t think about. A TV mount becomes a TV mount, hidden wires, and a soundbar. A fixture swap becomes a fixture swap plus a fan upgrade. You earn more per trip without finding a new customer.

Step 5: Protect your time and reputation

Watch for jobs that will blow up your schedule, like fixtures with hundreds of crystals, or repairs where a prior leak could get blamed on you. A handyman we know avoids faucets, disposals, and bidets for exactly that reason, so decide your own limits. Also check licensing: some states restrict plumbing and electrical work for handymen, so know your local rules before you sell those services.

Step 6: Keep learning

Learn from other tradespeople and add one new skill at a time. Tips travel fast in this business, so keep your eyes and ears open. Also, let your best-paying service guide what you learn next. It doesn’t make sense to learn how to do something that only earns a couple bucks.

Your 30-day starting plan

Week 1: Pick one or two niches and list the exact tools you need.

Week 2: Practice on friends’ or family’s homes, and time each job.

Week 3: Write a one-line offer and put it on your card, profile, and local groups.

Week 4: Quote your first five paid jobs with one add-on each, and ask each customer for a review.

Specializing is not about limiting your income. It is how you get faster, build trust, and charge more for the same hour of work.

item.title: Why Pay-Per-Lead Sites Cost More Than They Advertise
item.dc:creator: Bolt Answering Content Team
item.description: The price on a pay-per-lead invoice is rarely the price of a job. In most cases, you pay when a homeowner fills in a form, even if they are ready to start…
item.content:encoded:
The price on a pay-per-lead invoice is rarely the price of a job. In most cases, you pay when a homeowner fills in a form, even if they are ready to start or other contractors receive it.

One lead may be in many inboxes

In many lead-sale models, one homeowner request is sent to multiple contractors at once. So the moment you pay, you are racing others to a phone the homeowner may not answer.

The homeowner often filled in the form to see options, not to take a bunch of calls from contractors trying to pitch them. That mismatch explains why so many paid leads never pick up, or already have a bid in hand and only want a price check.

Cost per lead is the wrong number

The number that matters is cost per job won: total lead spend divided by jobs booked. Here is an illustrative example:

Plug in your own numbers. If a $40 lead turns into a $480 acquisition cost, the platform’s price tag was never the real price.

What contractors commonly report

Contractors who have bought leads describe a familiar pattern: prices that creep up, homeowners who never answer, leads that already have bids, and homeowners surprised to be called by several companies. Some describe trouble cancelling.

Regulators have also looked at the category. In January 2023 the FTC accepted a settlement with HomeAdvisor over allegations that it overstated how often its leads turned into jobs and misdescribed where some leads came from. The dispute ended in a $7.2 million settlement while the company did not admit wrongdoing (TechCrunch).

Read the terms before you buy

Before spending, ask three questions:

  1. Do you pay for leads that never answer?
  2. Can you cancel without a fee?
  3. Does the contract renew automatically?

Some contractors report being locked into multi-year agreements, or getting leads for the wrong kind of job. Get the answers in writing.

Keep the comparison fair, too. Google’s own Local Services Ads also charge per lead, so the same cost-per-job math applies there. Lead sites are not evil. They just should not be your only source, because you cannot control their price, their lead quality or how your reviews appear.

What to do instead

  1. Work out your cost per job won for every channel, using the table above.
  2. Put effort into channels you own: a clear website, a complete Google listing and steady reviews.
  3. Answer every call that comes in, from any source. A lead you never speak to cost money and returned nothing.

item.title: How Specializing Lets a Handyman Charge More
item.dc:creator: Bolt Answering Content Team
item.description: Specialists don’t compete on price. Here’s why getting really good at one or two jobs lets handymen charge more, and how bundling services adds revenue on…
item.content:encoded:
When you are known for one thing, customers stop comparing you against the cheapest person on a TaskRabbit. They are buying certainty. You have done this exact job dozens of times, you show up with the right parts and tools, and you finish quickly. Speed is the part many new handymen miss: the faster you are, the higher the hourly rate you can earn even if the customer pays a fair flat price.

Let the customer bring the materials

A good way to keep your take home rate higher is by making sure the client supplies the necessary product or materials, such as a TV, a faucet, or a smart doorbell. That keeps your costs down and removes the headache of buying, returning, and marking up parts. The profit margin goes up because you are selling labor and skill, not inventory.

Set expectations before you arrive

Certain projects require a lot more time and can put your profit at risk. Decorative light fixtures with endless crystals can eat an afternoon, so agree beforehand who assembles them. And on a garbage disposal install with a dishwasher, knocking out the knockout plug is easy to forget (… trust us, we’ve all done it), so build it into your checklist. Small misses like these cost you a free return visit and a bit of goodwill.

Bundle and offer solutions customers did not know they needed

When someone books a TV mount, ask whether they want the wires hidden in the wall, and whether they would like a soundbar installed at the same time. Customers rarely think about cable runs until the TV is up and the wire is dangling. Solving a problem they did not know they had is where the extra revenue comes from, and it makes the job feel like a better experience.

A reality check before you raise your rates

Treat the hourly numbers as a goal, not a promise, and check your local rules first. Remember, some plumbing and electrical work may be restricted by licensing, so look up what your state or city allows before advertising swaps like faucets, disposals, or light fixtures.

A simple pricing approach

  1. Pick one or two niches from the list in the previous post.
  2. Track how long each job really takes over your first ten jobs.
  3. Quote a flat price based on your fastest reliable time, plus a margin for surprises.
  4. Add an optional add-on to every quote, such as hidden wires or a second fixture.
  5. Raise your price once you are booked out for a few weeks.

item.title: The 5 Most Profitable Handyman Jobs You Can Start Offering Today
item.dc:creator: Bolt Answering Content Team
item.description: If you are still taking every random job that comes your way, you are probably leaving money on the table. The handymen who earn the most tend to pick a…
item.content:encoded:
If you are still taking every random job that comes your way, you are probably leaving money on the table. The handymen who earn the most tend to pick a small set of repeatable jobs, get fast at them, and let their reputation do the marketing. Here are five of the best places to start, counted down from five to one, with tips on what makes each one pay.

5. Drywall repair

Drywall is high skill but needs very little material to get started. Plenty of homeowners cannot fix a hole themselves, and plenty of homes have holes. It is hard at first, but every patch makes you faster, and once you are known as the person who makes walls disappear, referrals follow.

4. Door and lock installation

Replacing doorknobs and deadbolts is simple work that many people would rather not touch. Doors are one of the things in a house that constantly break or get damaged, so demand never dries up. The tool list is short, which keeps your profit margin high, and you can become the go-to door person in your neighborhood.

3. Ceiling fans and light fixtures

Most residential fans and fixtures are close to identical, so each install teaches you something that applies to the next one. One warning: a fixture the customer calls “easy” can turn out to have a thousand tiny parts, and hanging them can take hours. Settle up front who handles these intricate fixtures or price that job differently.

2. Faucets and garbage disposals

The theme here is swapping, not building. Pulling out a kitchen faucet and putting in a new one is far quicker than anything that involves construction. Disposals are similar, since the problem is often a tripped breaker, a clog, or a simple replacement.

1. TV mounting and smart home installs

This category is big enough that some people build whole businesses on it: TVs, soundbars, video doorbells, smart thermostats, and a growing list of connected appliances. The work is cleaner than drywall or plumbing, customers usually buy the equipment, and it feels like a specialist service. Bigger TVs may need a second person, but otherwise the barrier is low.

The common thread

All five jobs are fast to learn, need few tools, are easy to repeat, and often let the customer supply the materials. Pick one or two, get very good at them, and you stop competing as a generalist and start stuffing your pockets.
